options_ranked.title: Non-Anchor Engine Oils Cost Pass-Through Acceleration & Surcharge Pilot
options_ranked.description: Launch an immediate (0-90 day) pricing intervention that introduces base-oil cost-indexed surcharges and shortens the cost pass-through cadence on Engine Oils accounts that are NOT covered by the mid-quarter price-lock clause. This directly targets the Engine Oils product line decline (Δ-5.8pp, 26.03% vs 31.83% prior YTD) and its two worst-performing SKUs, Synthetic Blend (Δ-7.14pp) and Conventional Engine Oil (Δ-6.61pp), while explicitly excluding National Auto Parts Chain A and other price-locked anchor accounts from any list-price action.
options_ranked.rationale: Fastest, lowest-cost, most reversible lever available given the mid-quarter price-lock constraint; it does not require touching locked contracts and can be piloted within a single billing cycle.

arguments_for: Directly targets the largest single-product margin erosion (Synthetic Blend Engine Oil, Δ-7.14pp) via the confirmed cost-pass-through lag mechanism.
Low capital outlay relative to procurement or portfolio restructuring options, since it uses existing pricing infrastructure.
arguments_against: Recovery is capped because the largest, most price-locked accounts (e.g., National Auto Parts Chain A) cannot be repriced mid-quarter, limiting the addressable base.
Surcharge revenue may lag actual base-oil cost swings if internal approval cycles are slow, reproducing the same 1-month lag problem it aims to fix.
key_questions: What share of Engine Oils revenue sits with non-anchor accounts eligible for immediate surcharge action?

arguments_for: Preserves anchor account relationships by respecting the contractual price-lock, avoiding reputational or contractual risk.
Can be piloted on a subset of accounts to test price elasticity before wider rollout.
arguments_against: Non-anchor customers may push back or shift volume to competitors if surcharges are perceived as opportunistic without transparent base-oil index linkage.
Sales teams may face internal resistance to introducing a new pricing mechanism outside the standard renewal cycle.
key_questions: Which non-anchor Engine Oils accounts have the highest churn risk if a surcharge is introduced, and can they be excluded from the initial pilot?

implementation_triggers: Base oil index price exceeds a defined threshold for two consecutive months, confirming the cost-pass-through lag is active.
Non-anchor account tiering analysis identifies a sufficient revenue base (>X% of Engine Oils non-anchor revenue) to justify the pilot.
prerequisites: Legal/Contracts confirmation of which Engine Oils accounts fall outside the price-lock clause.
Finance sign-off on the surcharge index formula and cadence.

impact_estimate.basis: Surcharge/cadence acceleration on non-anchor Engine Oils accounts recovers a partial share of the -5.8pp Engine Oils product-line decline; this is a segment-level estimate since price-locked anchor accounts (including National Auto Parts Chain A) are excluded by constraint.
impact_estimate.scope_label: Engine Oils product line, non-anchor accounts

key_assumptions.assumption: Non-anchor Engine Oils accounts have sufficient contractual flexibility to accept surcharge adjustments within the current quarter.
key_assumptions.provenance: Contract terms audit confirming absence of price-lock clauses for the targeted non-anchor accounts.

key_assumptions.assumption: The ~1-month COGS pass-through lag identified in the causal register is the primary mechanism suppressing Engine Oils margin.
key_assumptions.provenance: Consistent with the confirmed causal edge: base oil price volatility passes through to COGS with a ~1-month lag before pricing catches up.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sales teams can implement surcharge mechanisms without material volume loss on targeted accounts.
key_assumptions.provenance: Post-implementation volume and win/loss tracking for surcharged accounts over the first two billing cycles.

options_ranked.title: Base Oil Procurement Consolidation & Hedging Program
options_ranked.description: Pursue a structural fix (3-12 months) targeting the root-cause dimension directly: renegotiate and consolidate base oil supply contracts and introduce hedging/index-lag reduction mechanisms to shorten the ~1-month COGS pass-through window. This addresses the confirmed causal edge (cogs<->gross_margin_pct) underlying the declines in Synthetic Blend Engine Oil (Δ-7.14pp), Conventional Engine Oil (Δ-6.61pp), Compressor Oil (Δ-5.86pp) and Hydraulic Oil (Δ-5.76pp), and is scoped to the International Division and Commercial & Industrial Division where the erosion is concentrated (Δ-4.98pp and Δ-4.71pp respectively), leaving segments 'within range' untouched.
options_ranked.rationale: Addresses the actual root-cause mechanism (confirmed causal edge) rather than symptom pricing, and has enterprise-wide reach across all base-oil-heavy products, not just Engine Oils.

arguments_for: Targets the confirmed, highest-confidence causal driver in the register (cogs<->gross_margin_pct, confirmed provenance), giving this option the strongest evidentiary grounding of the three.
Enterprise-wide reach touches all four major base-oil-heavy product decliners simultaneously, not just Engine Oils.
arguments_against: Procurement contract renegotiation typically requires multi-month lead time and may involve upfront hedging costs before any margin benefit materializes.
Savings are contingent on supplier willingness to offer improved terms, which is unverified and may require volume commitments that reduce future flexibility.
key_questions: What hedging or consolidation terms are realistically available from current or alternate base oil suppliers within two quarters?

arguments_for: Reduces exposure to future base-oil price volatility structurally, rather than requiring repeated tactical pricing responses.
Can be piloted in International Division and Commercial & Industrial Division first, limiting operational disruption before wider rollout.
arguments_against: Supplier consolidation concentrates supply risk; a single-supplier disruption could create a new operational vulnerability.
It is unverified whether Compressor Oil and Hydraulic Oil share the same base-oil cost structure as Engine Oils, so the procurement fix may not fully reach those SKUs.
key_questions: Does the base oil input share for Compressor Oil and Hydraulic Oil match Engine Oils closely enough for the same procurement fix to apply?

implementation_triggers: Procurement identifies at least one alternate/consolidated supplier offering index terms superior to current contracts.
Finance confirms hedging instruments are available at acceptable cost for base oil exposure.
prerequisites: Product-level COGS decomposition confirming base oil as a material input share for Compressor Oil and Hydraulic Oil, not just Engine Oils.
Procurement RFP process completed with at least two alternate suppliers.

impact_estimate.basis: Shortening the confirmed base-oil-to-COGS pass-through lag recovers a portion of the enterprise's -4.49pp YTD gross margin decline by reducing the absorption window across the four largest product-level decliners (combined Δ range -5.76 to -7.14pp).

key_assumptions.assumption: Base oil procurement consolidation/hedging can materially shorten or offset the current cost pass-through lag.
key_assumptions.provenance: Consistent with the confirmed causal mechanism that base oil price volatility drives the lag; procurement renegotiation directly targets that lag.

key_assumptions.assumption: Compressor Oil and Hydraulic Oil margin declines share the same base-oil cost driver as Engine Oils.
key_assumptions.provenance: Product-level COGS decomposition confirming base oil as a material (e.g., >40%) input cost share for Compressor and Hydraulic Oil.

key_assumptions.assumption: Suppliers will offer improved terms without long-term volume commitments that erode future negotiating leverage.
key_assumptions.provenance: Signed procurement contract terms post-negotiation compared against current baseline pricing.

options_ranked.title: Contract Renewal Repricing & Phased Portfolio Rationalization (International & Commercial/Industrial Divisions)
options_ranked.description: A 12+ month strategic play with two explicit phases. Phase 1 (deferred, respecting the mid-quarter price-lock constraint): introduce base-oil cost-indexed pricing clauses at contract RENEWAL (not mid-term) for anchor accounts, and rationalize the lowest-margin, lowest-volume SKUs within Compressor Oil and Hydraulic Oil in International Division (Δ-4.98pp) and Commercial & Industrial Division (Δ-4.71pp). Phase 2 — mix acceleration toward Synthetic Blend Engine Oil — is explicitly NOT started until Option 2 restores Synthetic Blend's margin baseline: the data shows Synthetic Blend is currently the WORST performer (Δ-7.14pp, 20.64% vs 27.78% prior), so shifting volume toward it today would compound the problem rather than solve it. The resolution path is: restore Synthetic Blend margin via base-oil cost actions first, then accelerate premium mix once its margin has recovered above the current baseline.
options_ranked.rationale: Provides a durable, contractually-compliant pricing structure for the future while avoiding the trap of shifting volume toward a currently underperforming premium mix; but it is slow, higher-cost, and carries revenue-at-risk from SKU rationalization.

arguments_for: Builds a permanent, cost-indexed pricing structure that reduces recurrence of margin erosion at every future renewal cycle, unlike one-time tactical fixes.
SKU rationalization removes structurally low-margin, low-volume products from International Division and Commercial & Industrial Division, improving blended margin mechanically.
arguments_against: The premium_mix_pct<->gross_margin_pct relationship this option ultimately relies on is an unconfirmed template prior, not a validated fact, so the Phase 2 upside is uncertain.
12-18 month time-to-value means no near-term relief for the current -4.49pp YTD decline.
key_questions: What is the revenue-at-risk from rationalizing low-margin SKUs in International Division and Commercial & Industrial Division, and does it exceed the projected margin gain?

arguments_for: Explicitly defers all anchor-account price changes to contract renewal, ensuring full compliance with the mid-quarter price-lock clause.
Sequencing Phase 2 behind Option 2's cost restoration avoids the documented contradiction of shifting volume toward a currently worse-performing product.
arguments_against: Contract renewal dates for anchor accounts (including National Auto Parts Chain A) are not in the dataset, so the earliest compliant repricing window is unverified.
Portfolio rationalization is low-reversibility; if customer attrition exceeds projections, lost revenue cannot be easily recovered.
key_questions: When do the anchor account contracts (including National Auto Parts Chain A) come up for renewal, and does that timeline align with the Phase 1 rollout?

implementation_triggers: Option 2 demonstrates measurable Synthetic Blend Engine Oil margin recovery for two consecutive periods, unlocking Phase 2 mix acceleration.
Anchor account renewal calendar confirms compliant repricing windows within the next two quarters.
prerequisites: Contract renewal-date calendar for all anchor accounts, including National Auto Parts Chain A.
Customer retention risk assessment for proposed SKU rationalization in International Division and Commercial & Industrial Division.
Confirmation that Option 2 has restored Synthetic Blend Engine Oil margin before Phase 2 begins.

impact_estimate.basis: Contract-renewal repricing plus SKU rationalization scoped to International Division and Commercial & Industrial Division (combined Δ-4.98pp and Δ-4.71pp exposure) targets their margin erosion directly; the premium-mix acceleration component is deferred and excluded from this near-term range pending Synthetic Blend margin restoration under Option 2.

key_assumptions.assumption: Anchor account contracts have renewal windows within the next 12 months allowing repricing without breaching the mid-quarter price-lock clause.
key_assumptions.provenance: Contract management system query returning renewal dates for National Auto Parts Chain A and other anchor accounts.

key_assumptions.assumption: Once base-oil-driven margin erosion in Synthetic Blend Engine Oil is resolved, accelerating its mix share will positively move blended margin.
key_assumptions.provenance: Consistent with the unconfirmed template prior that premium mix (Synthetic Blend, High Mileage) carries structurally higher margin; falsified if margin fails to move with mix share after cost restoration.

key_assumptions.assumption: SKU rationalization in International Division and Commercial & Industrial Division will not trigger material customer attrition.
key_assumptions.provenance: Customer retention tracking for rationalized SKUs across two quarters post-implementation.

flagged_side_effects: Potential customer attrition in rationalized SKUs before margin benefit is realized.
Deferring Phase 2 mix acceleration may frustrate commercial teams eager to push the historically higher-margin Synthetic Blend line.

problem_reframe.situation: Gross margin_pct has declined 4.49 percentage points year-to-date on an overall basis (29.94% vs. 34.43% prior YTD), the net effect across the entire Lubricants Business portfolio.
problem_reframe.complication: The decline is not uniform: it is concentrated in five segments — International Division (Δ-4.98pp), Commercial & Industrial Division (Δ-4.71pp), Service Centers Division (Δ-4.38pp), Retail Products Division (Δ-4.26pp), and National Auto Parts Chain A — and in base-oil-heavy products (Synthetic Blend Engine Oil Δ-7.14pp, Conventional Engine Oil Δ-6.61pp, Compressor Oil Δ-5.86pp, Hydraulic Oil Δ-5.76pp, Engine Oils product line Δ-5.8pp), while the scqa_summary confirms 'remaining segments are within range.' Two fiscal periods (2026-006/007/008) show unusually large positive deltas (+31 to +32pp) flagged simultaneously as 'within threshold,' an unreconciled anomaly that should not be treated as a genuine improvement signal.
problem_reframe.question: What operational interventions can recover margin in the confirmed base-oil-driven product and divisional decliners without breaching the contractual price-lock on Lubricants anchor accounts, while preserving the segments that are already performing within range?
key_assumptions: The confirmed cogs<->gross_margin_pct causal edge (base oil price volatility passing through to COGS with a ~1-month lag) is the dominant mechanism behind the Engine Oils and Compressor Oil declines, not a one-off input.
Segments not named in the top change points (outside the five confirmed decliners) are genuinely stable and do not require intervention.
The anomalous +31 to +32pp period deltas in 2026-006/007/008 are a data or period-definition artifact rather than a real margin swing.

unresolved_tensions.tension: Accelerating surcharges on non-anchor Engine Oils accounts (Option 1) risks customer pushback or volume loss precisely on the accounts that are not contractually protected, creating a trade-off between speed and commercial risk.
unresolved_tensions.requires: VP Sales to complete a customer-tier risk assessment identifying which non-anchor Engine Oils accounts can absorb a surcharge without churn risk, before rollout (target: Week 3).

unresolved_tensions.tension: Option 3's anchor-account repricing is deferred to contract renewal to respect the price-lock clause, but the renewal timing is unknown, creating uncertainty about when structural pricing relief becomes available versus the urgency of the current -4.49pp decline.
unresolved_tensions.requires: Commercial Contracts Manager to produce a renewal-date calendar for all anchor accounts, flagging which fall within the next two quarters (by Week 2).

unresolved_tensions.tension: It is unverified whether Compressor Oil and Hydraulic Oil margin declines share the same base-oil cost driver as Engine Oils, which determines whether Option 2's procurement fix actually reaches those products or only partially addresses the enterprise decline.
unresolved_tensions.requires: Finance Controller to run a product-level COGS decomposition for Compressor Oil and Hydraulic Oil isolating base-oil input share (by Week 4).

problem_reframe.situation: Gross margin_pct has declined 4.49 percentage points year-to-date on an overall basis (29.94% vs. 34.43% prior YTD), the net effect across the entire Lubricants Business portfolio.
problem_reframe.complication: The decline is not uniform: it is concentrated in five segments — International Division (Δ-4.98pp), Commercial & Industrial Division (Δ-4.71pp), Service Centers Division (Δ-4.38pp), Retail Products Division (Δ-4.26pp), and National Auto Parts Chain A — and in base-oil-heavy products (Synthetic Blend Engine Oil Δ-7.14pp, Conventional Engine Oil Δ-6.61pp, Compressor Oil Δ-5.86pp, Hydraulic Oil Δ-5.76pp, Engine Oils product line Δ-5.8pp), while the scqa_summary confirms 'remaining segments are within range.' Two fiscal periods (2026-006/007/008) show unusually large positive deltas (+31 to +32pp) flagged simultaneously as 'within threshold,' an unreconciled anomaly that should not be treated as a genuine improvement signal.
problem_reframe.question: What operational interventions can recover margin in the confirmed base-oil-driven product and divisional decliners without breaching the contractual price-lock on Lubricants anchor accounts, while preserving the segments that are already performing within range?
key_assumptions: The confirmed cogs<->gross_margin_pct causal edge (base oil price volatility passing through to COGS with a ~1-month lag) is the dominant mechanism behind the Engine Oils and Compressor Oil declines, not a one-off input.
Segments not named in the top change points (outside the five confirmed decliners) are genuinely stable and do not require intervention.
The anomalous +31 to +32pp period deltas in 2026-006/007/008 are a data or period-definition artifact rather than a real margin swing.
